pages.name: One fault already there
pages.text: Here is a 440 V insulated board with two feeders. A first fault already joins feeder 1's L1 to the hull. The alarm is lit. Nothing has tripped and both motors run. As in the shifting triangle, the hull has moved to L1. So L2 and L3 now sit 440 V from the hull, on every circuit. Only their insulation holds them off it.

A first fault joins feeder 1's L1 to motor 1's frame, so the hull now sits at L1's voltage, and the earth alarm is lit. There is no second fault. Neither breaker reaches its instant trip.

pages.name: An earth fault, earthed
pages.task: Leave this board for a moment. On an earthed 254 V supply, a circuit's Zs is 0.4 Ω. What current flows in a solid earth fault?
pages.why: I = U0 ÷ Zs = 254 ÷ 0.4 = 635 A, on that earthed supply. Feeder 1 on this insulated board has the same 0.4 Ω loop. The same rule will size its second fault.

pages.name: Which trips nothing?
pages.task: Feeder 1's L1 is already faulted to the hull. Which second fault on feeder 2 trips nothing?
pages.why: The hull already sits at L1. A second join from L1 to the hull has no voltage across it, so it drives no loop.[^1] It still needs finding and clearing.

pages.task: Feeder 1's L1 and feeder 2's L2 are both faulted to the hull. What voltage drives the loop?

pages.name: Two loops end to end
pages.text: The current runs through both circuits, one after the other. Feeder 2's loop is its L2 out and its protective conductor back. Feeder 1's is its L1 and its protective conductor. So the loop impedance is Z1 + Z2. When the circuits match, that is double one circuit's loop impedance.[^2] With 0.4 Ω each, 440 ÷ 0.8 = 550 A. Say each breaker trips instantly at 400 A. Both carry the 550 A, past each trip mark.

pages.name: Loops of 0.4 and 0.6 Ω
pages.task: Feeder 1's loop is 0.4 Ω and feeder 2's is 0.6 Ω. A second fault strikes feeder 2's L3. What current flows?
pages.why: The loop runs through both circuits, so it is 0.4 + 0.6 = 1.0 Ω. The current is 440 ÷ 1.0 = 440 A.

pages.name: A week with the alarm on
pages.task: The alarm has shown a first fault on L1 for a week. Nothing has tripped and every motor runs. What is the risk now?
pages.answer: One failure on L2 or L3, anywhere, makes a short through the hull
pages.why: L2 and L3 have held line voltage to the hull all week, on every circuit. One insulation failure on either joins it to L1 through the hull. So a first fault should be cleared with the shortest practicable delay.[^3]

pages.name: Earthed against insulated
pages.task: Two circuits each have a 0.4 Ω loop. On an earthed 254 V supply, one of them passes 635 A in an earth fault. On the insulated 440 V board, what does a second fault through both pass?
pages.why: 440 ÷ 0.8 = 550 A. The voltage is 1.73 times higher, but the loop impedance is doubled.[^2] So the current is about 0.87 times the earthed figure.

A first fault joins feeder 1's L1 to motor 1's frame, so the hull now sits at L1's voltage, and the earth alarm is lit. A second fault joins feeder 2's L2 to motor 2's frame. pages.name: Which motors can stop?
pages.task: Both loops are 0.4 Ω, and each breaker trips instantly at 400 A. A second fault strikes feeder 2's L3. Which motors can stop?
pages.answer: Either or both, as both breakers carry 550 A
pages.why: One current runs round the whole loop, so both breakers carry 550 A. Whichever opens first clears the short, and both may open. So a second fault can stop two circuits, including the one with the first fault.
